progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B5a: a chromosome is one long DNA molecule carrying many genes; homologous pairs; diploid 46 in humans; centromere; counting chromosomes by centromeres. From B5b: meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair and cross over in prophase I, partners separate in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II, gametes are haploid, fertilisation restores the diploid number. From B9: autosomes and a coded karyotype strip (22 numbered pairs and the sex chromosomes). From b01: a mutation is a change in DNA; it can make new alleles. From b02: ionising radiation breaks both strands, and broken ends joined back wrongly can lose or swap a piece (b02 scene 6 named "later video"). From b03: point mutations (substitution, insertion, deletion; silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift). Not assumed: chromosomal mutation, the four structural types, gene dosage, balanced rearrangement, nondisjunction, trisomy, karyotype as evidence of number.
progression.startsWith: Change chromosome structure or number. The video opens: In 1959, Jérôme Lejeune, Marthe Gautier and Raymond Turpin looked at dividing cells from children with Down syndrome, and counted their chromosomes.
progression.stopsAfter: defining a chromosomal mutation as a change in chromosome structure or number that can affect many genes at once, and contrasting its scale with a point mutation; explaining two causes of structural change (breaks rejoined wrongly; unequal crossing over, which makes a duplication and a deletion together); describing deletion (genes lost), duplication (extra copies, changed gene dosage; Bar eye), inversion (segment reversed) and translocation (segment moved to a non-matching chromosome); explaining that balanced inversions and translocations keep every gene, so carriers are often healthy, but breakpoints can disrupt or reactivate genes (the chromosome 9 and 22 leukaemia) and a carrier's gametes can be unbalanced; explaining nondisjunction in meiosis and trisomy; explaining trisomy 21 as extra dosage of normal genes and why it is survivable; comparing point and chromosomal mutations on cause, process and effect, including that size does not fix severity; applying this to an unseen HSC-style chromosome diagram and to a sickle cell against Down syndrome comparison.
progression.nextLesson: which mutations can be passed to the next generation, and does it matter where they happen (route entry bio-m6-b05).

teaching.task: A chromosomal mutation can change hundreds of genes without spelling a single base wrong, so what exactly changes, and why does that affect a whole organism?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a chromosomal mutation affects many genes (one chromosome carries hundreds, 2); how structure changes (breaks rejoined wrongly; out-of-step crossing over, 3); why a deletion is often lethal (one copy left, 4); why a duplication matters (more copies, more product, 4); why a balanced carrier is often healthy (every gene still there, 5) and when not (breakpoints, 5); why the carrier's children may be affected (unbalanced gametes, 6); how an extra chromosome arises (a pair fails to separate, 7); why trisomy 21 affects many systems (extra dosage of hundreds of normal genes, 8) and why it is survivable (smallest chromosome, 8). Visible case: one HSC-style chromosome with genes A to H carries every structural type; one karyotype strip carries the count. Video advantage: segments visibly drop, double, flip and swap; partner bars line up out of step; the pair fails to separate and the counts change. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every given on screen. Reading load: normal and changed bars stacked, at most about three tags; the attempt 1 card is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: The 1959 count of 47 chromosomes sets the surprise (normal genes, one extra chromosome); a chromosomal mutation is shown as a change to a whole bar of genes, contrasted in scale with a point mutation; breaks rejoined wrongly and unequal crossing over show how structure changes before each type is named; deletion and duplication change content and dosage (Bar eye), inversion and translocation change order and position (one leukaemia); a balanced carrier's gametes show the next-generation catch; nondisjunction is followed through the meiosis strip to an extra or missing chromosome; trisomy 21 is explained as normal genes at extra dosage; point and chromosomal mutations are compared by cause, process and effect; the book of chapters analogy carries the memory. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, then the decision rule hands off to where a mutation happens (b05).
teaching.openingDecision: In 1959, Jérôme Lejeune, Marthe Gautier and Raymond Turpin looked at dividing cells from children with Down syndrome, and counted their chromosomes. Their cells had forty-seven, one more than the usual forty-six. The extra one was small, later named chromosome twenty-one. Its genes weren't faulty. There was simply an extra copy of every one of them. So how can extra, missing or rearranged pieces of chromosome change a whole organism?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is an HSC-style diagram item: a normal chromosome (A B C, centromere, D E F G H) and a non-matching chromosome (M N, centromere, O P Q), with three changed versions, 1 (A B C D E F E F G H), 2 (A B C D G F E H) and 3 (A B C D E F P Q with M N O G H). Name each mutation, then identify which change alters the number of copies of a gene in the cell, with a reason. It tests reading a diagram gene by gene and the dosage idea. 11c is a compare item: sickle cell disease (a substitution in the beta-globin gene) against Down syndrome (usually an extra chromosome 21), compared on how each arises, how much DNA each changes and its effect. It tests the dotpoint's own "compare causes, processes and effects" across b03 and b04. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: "compare the causes, processes and effects of different types of mutation, including but not limited to:" with the examples "point mutation" and "chromosomal mutation". This video owns the chromosomal half (causes: breaks rejoined wrongly, unequal crossing over, nondisjunction; processes: the four structural types and changes in number; effects: gene content, dosage, order, position, breakpoints) and the comparison with point mutation that the dotpoint's verb asks for (scene 9, attempt 2). Update the ledger row for B6-IQ1-02 (shared with b01 and b03) when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: One chromosome board, drawn the way HSC papers draw chromosomes: a long rounded bar with a narrowed centromere (b05a's `ChromBar` look, cream fill, ink outline), thin bands across it, and gene letters A to H printed in small serif type beside their bands; a second, non-matching chromosome is a shorter bar in a pale blue-grey with letters M to Q. A moving or changed segment is shaded amber and slides, flips or doubles on its spoken word; a lost segment drops away as a dashed outline. Before and after are always stacked (normal above, changed below) so the change is read by comparison, as in an exam diagram. A coded karyotype strip (B9's: 22 numbered pairs plus X and X, drawn as small banded bars in pairs) carries the counts in the hook and scene 8; pair 21 holds three bars there. A meiosis strip for scene 7 uses B5b's model cell drawing (one pair, plum and teal, as in B5b) through meiosis I to four gametes, with counts under each cell. Real objects are painted: the microscope (`m6-microscope-v1.png`), a stained chromosome spread as seen down a microscope (new plate), the painted chromosome close-up (`b5x-zoom-chromosome-v1.png`) as the bridge from the real object to the coded bar, and the fruit flies (`m5x-fly-red-eye-v1.png`, new Bar and double-Bar plates). No people: the hook uses the microscope and the cell spread, never a child or a patient. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three text items on screen at once besides the gene letters; each tag fades when the next cue lands; the karyotype strip and the meiosis strip leave when their scenes end.
design.transitionPlan: The microscope plate and karyotype strip open the hook; the painted chromosome close-up crossfades into the coded GeneBar, the bridge from the real object; the chromosome board then stacks normal above changed for each type, with the amber segment sliding, flipping, doubling or dropping away on its word; the carrier's cell splits into two gametes; the meiosis strip replaces the bars for nondisjunction and the hook's karyotype strip returns for trisomy 21; the CompareBoard gathers both families in two columns; the book outline sits beside the GeneBar for memory; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
